Name: eos_thinking_stop_decision
Title: Knowing When to Stop: The Circuit Behind the End-of-Thinking Decision
Short Hypothesis: The decision to end the thinking phase (emit </think>) is controlled by an identifiable mechanism integrating commitment and verification-completion signals; this stop-decision circuit is often mis-timed (too late), and correcting its threshold yields efficient stopping.
Related Work: Budget forcing (Muennighoff et al. 2025 s1) externally controls stopping; we study the model's internal stop-decision circuit and its mis-calibration, enabling internal rather than forced control.
Abstract: Reasoning models mark the end of thinking with a special token, but the mechanism deciding when to stop is opaque and often lets thinking run long. We hypothesize a stop-decision circuit that integrates commitment (answer decided) and verification-completion signals to trigger the end-of-thinking token, and that this circuit is systematically biased toward late stopping (a learned safety margin). We localize the circuit by contrasting activations at genuine stop points versus matched non-stop positions and by patching to the end-of-thinking logit. We measure the circuit's readiness signal over the trace and compare it to independent 'answer stable' ground truth to quantify late-stopping bias. We then test threshold correction: lowering the internal stop threshold (via steering the stop direction) to end thinking at true readiness, measuring accuracy versus tokens against budget-forcing baselines. We analyze whether the safety margin protects hard problems, revealing a difficulty-dependent optimal threshold. This exposes the internal control of thinking termination and turns it into a calibrated efficiency knob.
Experiments: 1. Locate stop-decision components via contrast at end-of-thinking vs non-stop positions; patch to </think> logit. 2. Extract stop-readiness signal; compare to answer-stability ground truth to measure late-stop bias. 3. Threshold correction via steering the stop direction; accuracy vs tokens vs budget forcing (s1-style). 4. Difficulty-dependent optimal threshold analysis. 5. Safety check on hard/adversarial items. 6. Cross-model validation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Stop decision may be distributed and hard to localize. Lowering the threshold could harm hard problems where the margin is protective. Steering the stop direction may have side effects. Requires models with explicit thinking delimiters. Late-stop bias may vary by training recipe.
